subject: ent
title: Carcinoma of the larynx

steps.tx: Laryngeal cancer is usually **squamous cell carcinoma** caused by smoking and alcohol use. The **glottic** region involves the true vocal cords, has sparse lymphatics, presents with early hoarseness, and carries the best prognosis. The **supraglottic** region has rich lymphatics, presents late with sore throat, referred ear pain and neck nodes, and carries a worse prognosis. The subglottic region is rarest and presents late with stridor. Any hoarseness beyond three weeks in a smoker needs laryngoscopy, and vocal cord mobility grades tumour depth because fixation signals deep muscle invasion.
steps.say: Most cancers of the voice box develop from smoking and alcohol and show squamous cell type. Tumours of the true cords produce hoarseness early and involve nodes late, so they allow the best outlook. Tumours above the cords remain silent longer and reach neck nodes early through rich lymph channels. Any smoker with hoarseness lasting more than three weeks requires examination of the larynx with a scope. A fixed vocal cord indicates deep invasion of muscle and raises the tumour stage.

vis.alt: Diagram showing laryngeal subsites: supraglottic, glottic, subglottic, and their lymphatic drainage.
vis.caption: Laryngeal subsites and lymphatic drainage

steps.tx: Workup starts with flexible and operative laryngoscopy with **biopsy** of the lesion. **Contrast CT or MRI** of the larynx and neck maps cartilage invasion and spread into the pre epiglottic and paraglottic spaces. Chest imaging looks for a second primary tumour or distant spread, with nutrition, dental, speech, swallow and smoking cessation review. Transglottic tumours cross the ventricle and ignore subsite borders. HPV plays only a minor role here, unlike in oropharyngeal cancer. **Leukoplakia** and dysplasia of the cords are premalignant lesions that need regular surveillance.
steps.say: Doctors confirm the diagnosis by viewing the larynx with a scope and taking a tissue sample. Scans of the neck reveal cartilage destruction and spread into spaces around the voice box. Imaging of the chest searches for another primary cancer or distant deposits, because smokers carry that added risk. The team also reviews nutrition, teeth, speech, swallowing, and supports quitting smoking. Tumours that cross the ventricle ignore subsite borders. White patches on the cords need watchful follow up, and HPV matters far less here than in throat cancer.

steps.tx: The scope view shows an **ulcerated glottic tumour** on one cord with the epiglottis above and the arytenoid below, matching the workup step where every lesion needs biopsy. The panel grades **cord mobility** from normal through impaired to fixed, because fixation upstages the tumour toward T3 disease. In the exam, link a fixed cord with deep muscle invasion and cartilage spread, which favours **contrast CT or MRI** mapping before the treatment choice is made.
steps.say: This scope view presents an ulcerated cancer of one vocal cord with the epiglottis above and the arytenoid below. The key helps learners grade cord movement from normal through impaired to fixed. A fixed cord indicates deep muscle invasion and raises the stage toward advanced disease. Such cases require contrast scans that map cartilage spread before doctors choose between organ preservation and removal.

vis.alt: Laryngoscopy showing ulcerated glottic squamous carcinoma on left cord, with epiglottis, true cord, arytenoid and T staging note
vis.caption: Laryngoscopic glottic squamous carcinoma with cord staging key. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Early glottic cancer is cured equally well by **radiotherapy** or **transoral laser surgery**, using a single modality that preserves the larynx. Advanced disease forces a choice between **total laryngectomy** and organ preservation with concurrent cisplatin and radiation. Laryngectomy leaves a permanent stoma and needs voice rehabilitation through a tracheoesophageal prosthesis, electrolarynx, or oesophageal speech. Combined treatment spares anatomy in many patients, with surgery reserved for failure, but a preserved larynx with aspiration can fare worse. The decision is multidisciplinary and weighs patient values, lung reserve, and salvage options.
steps.say: Small cancers limited to the vocal cords are cured either with radiation or with laser removal through the mouth. Both options involve one method alone and aim to preserve the voice box. Larger cancers require either complete removal of the larynx or combined chemotherapy and radiation that tries to save the organ. After removal, patients depend on a permanent neck opening for breathing. They need new ways of speaking and can choose a valve, a device, or gullet speech. Combined treatment often keeps the structure working, with surgery kept in reserve for failure. A saved larynx that constantly aspirates may serve the patient worse than removal.

steps.tx: Airway safety comes first in advanced disease, so impending obstruction needs **awake tracheostomy** before treatment begins. After laryngectomy, patients need stoma education because speech needs a prosthesis, water can flood the airway, and heat moisture exchangers protect the trachea. Follow up watches for hypothyroidism after neck radiation and for **pharyngocutaneous fistula** after salvage surgery, especially with prior radiation or poor nutrition. **Elective neck treatment** covers both sides in supraglottic cancer even when nodes feel normal, because hidden spread is common, while early glottic cancer needs neck observation alone.
steps.say: Securing the airway remains the priority when a large tumour blocks breathing. Surgeons usually perform a planned tracheostomy while the patient remains awake. After removal of the larynx, nurses guide stoma care and daily cleaning. Voice needs an artificial valve, and water must never enter the opening. Doctors later check thyroid function after radiation. They assess the wound for a leak between the throat and the skin, particularly after salvage operations. Cancers above the cords require treatment to both sides of the neck even when no nodes are felt. Early cord cancers need observation of the neck alone.
